      I recently asked AI to help me look through the latest Windows binaries for undocumented features and functionality. Among the leads it turned up, one list immediately caught my attention: coding agents such as codex.exe, claude.exe, copilot.exe, and cursor.exe, alongside familiar developer tools such as python.exe, dotnet.exe, gcc.exe, and code.exe.Why would a Windows system DLL need a list of coding agents and developer tools?The names were in MissionControlAggregator.dll. I asked the agent to follow the references and dig into what the DLL actually does. That led from a handful of string comparisons to a running Windows component that records which coding agents and developer tools have been used, saves that information locally, and reports it to Windows Diagnostics. title: If an App Asks for Full Disk Access or System and App Protection Override (support.apple.com)
comments:
This is a very poorly conceived API. If developers' use cases don't fit cleanly into Apple's (narrow) idea about how a hypothetical app should work, developers will continue to feel like they need to request these expansive permissions. A good filesystem permission API could include any of these which would make users WAY safer and enable developers to request far smaller scopes:- Allow the developer to specify the common location(s) that they need access to. Rather than having to have the user select the folder they want to grant access to, have the developer say "this app uses data in these 5 folders, do you want to grant that access" - so much clearer, and useful in cases where an app has to integrate with other apps through the filesystem.
- Readonly access. Allow an app to read your files but prevent writes or deletes.
- Time limited access. Allow some kind of access and allow the user to auto-expire it rather than having to remember it exists.
- Allow for negative access (i.e. allow labels or tags on directories to mark them as sensitive and prevent access by default - browsers could do this for their cookie stores, `~/.ssh` could ship with it as a default, etc.)Apple could have used this opportunity to think through the question of "why do developers ask for filesystem access, and how can we allow legitimate usage through well scoped access controls", but instead they built a bad API that will (I would guess) not actually allow developers to be more judicious or achieve any of the user-safety benefits.Apple needs to learn to talk to (and listen to) developers.reply

Developers are important, but Apple understands that it must ultimately prioritise non-technical end users as their highest priority. Apple's approach puts control in users' hands rather than allowing developers to define the scope of access. Moving from Full Disk Access to user-selected folders is a significant security improvement, even if the API doesn't accommodate every developer use case.It's also critical to recognise that data exfiltration is just as serious a risk as data manipulation. Read-only access doesn't prevent data theft, and time-limited access can't undo it.reply

What's common about it?I'm so not sure they need access to anything yet.I use Spotify, Slack, Zoom, and WhatsApp: All of them have asked for it, but they all seem to work fine if I deny them access to full-disk access. So I am confident your issue is a non-issue for me and millions of people like me.I don't have any apps that need this, so I do not want you to blow past this so quickly with the prior that just because you are a developer who has a use case that requires this, it is still my computer and you don't get any time on it while you're asking for this.> Readonly access. Allow an app to read your files but prevent writes or deletesAgain: Absolutely not. There are no files I want your app to have access to without an explanation.> Allow for negative access (i.e. allow labels or tags on directories to mark them as sensitive and prevent access by default - browsers could do this for their cookie stores, `~/.ssh` could ship with it as a default, etc.)I know Linux works this way, and it only ever works for stuff that the integrator ships (i.e. on Red Hat, they are called seLinux labels), so it's not something that independent publishers have ever done, and to my knowledge, despite it being so easy, not one independent developer has ever used them in the way you say, despite such a thing being possible for more than 25 years.> Apple needs to learn to talk to (and listen to) developers.That sounds like your opinion. I think developers need to explain better what they actually want and why.You have what you ask for on other platforms, so I think if your ideas were so right you would have simply ignored Apple, so I think Apple doesn't need to do shit for you, and you have some explaining to do.reply

By default, an unsandboxed program can access everything except specific protected directories, and can request access to those directories too, e.g. Documents, Desktop, Photos, other apps' data.Full Disk Access is the last resort that turns all of that off.  Or, well, was.It's also the only way to access Messages, which might be why certain AI apps request it.reply

first_paragraph: Starting in macOS 27.3, when some apps ask for Full Disk Access or System & App Protection Override, you have the option to choose only specific protected folders or apps for the app to access. This puts you in control of what data is accessible to the app.Apps that might ask for Full Disk Access or System & App Protection Override include backup apps, disk cleaners, file indexers, security apps, and others. While some of these apps operate best when granted broader access, others may ask for the same level of access even when they don't need it. title: Running coding agents without handing them my credentials (antonio.cx)
comments: I just don’t think I agree with these designs at all. Everyone seems to be super laser focused on “not allowing their AI to have keys” when basically giving their AI direct access to what the keys enable, optionally adding a layer of ceremony in front where you tap “approve”. I’m looking at the alert that is shown there and I don’t see anything that makes me feel like it allows for an informed choice at the time of it popping up. So then, what’s the benefit?reply

As much as I wanted to say you’re wrong, you’re right. After reading TFA, the security boundary is not sound.Wanting agents to act like you is wrong. You need to own that trust boundary. Build whatever tooling satisfies the contract that agents should have a “not”+<you> (or <you>+”-agent”) identity, and you actuate across that boundary explicitly.For example, I have a second agent GitHub account that points at my human one. That allows me to write a trusted proxy that ACLs its identity tightly.It cannot write to public repos ever. In the worst possible case, it externalizes to a private repo’s issue tracker. (Still has never happened in ~4 months)Once you have this, you can let agents run free. But, it isn’t trivial to set up. Moreover, people don’t want to “do the work.”All this assumes you abide by “never run untrusted agents on trusted hardware.”reply

I would certainly prefer having separate credentials with permissions limited to what I want to allow the agent to do. However I have run into two problems with that.The first, and bigger, issue is that some services either don't have have suffiently fine control over permissions, so in order to grant permission to do useful things, I also have to allow it to do dangerous things, or I don't have a way to create a more limited access token at all. I wish that it was more common to allow creating short-lived, limited accces personal access tokens for services.The smaller issue is that sometimes I do want the agent to do something more risky with my approval, and provide me with sufficient context to make an informed decision. That can sort of be worked around though by telling it to just give me the command to run, then I can audit and run it myself.reply

Basically these designs are meant to protect the key from leaking i.e. if agent holds key, prompt injections can happen.If agent never holds the key, then the risk profile changes.But you're right that it's a different problem to what access the key has and that's a different problem usually solved by having narrower keys or etc.disclaimer: I work on smolvm which does this at the networking layer and argued with myself on this too.reply

Sure, my view on this is more or less that often the setup that creates this kind of situation often allows the agent to effectively mint a new key anyway. For example, if you have my browser cookie or something I may not want my agent to leak this on the web, but if I use it to authenticate network requests to the service transparently the model can just go into the account page and change my password or something, then leak that. In general it is not safe to hand an agent access to a service which is designed for human interaction and assume that it was properly secured such that persistent, transferrable access is not something that can be generated.reply

As Cursor generously demonstrated for the whole world, long-lived credentials in LLM transcripts are an attack path.Your transcript passes in plain-text through a chain of token and compute resellers. And you have no good way of knowing who those companies are and what type of "observability" they deploy.reply

>if agent holds key, prompt injections can happen.I just rotate keys? And preload them with $$$. Following the same pragmatic advice that served me well trading crypto. Only gamble with what you are willing to lose.reply

I'm trying to address this w/ clank.talk: a self-discoverable scripting language for agents that replaces bash with a controlled sandbox environment and strives to be easy for humans to read:https://clank.talkI'm designing this for the student AI infrastructure here at Montana State, to avoid rolling out the current wild-west of local agents to our student body.reply

AppleScript lives again? ;) I think it's an interesting concept, but it's really hard to do right. There are a lot of things that require very careful accounting for even in such a design–I see that you are already blocking access to .git for example, since the agent can drop code there that makes safe-looking commands like git status unsafe. This is definitely something I've been looking at, as well as taint tracking, it's just really hard. Would be interested to see where you take it!reply

title: Why did modems have speakers? (2019) (retrocomputing.stackexchange.com)
comments: The general name for this is mechanical sympathy. Humans have advanced sensory processing abilities, and if we design systems that use them, the performance of the humans operating the system improves.It improves for the simple reason that richer feedback leads to a better understanding of the state of the system, which in turn lets the operator predict the effects of their actions more accurately.I thinkn we could be a lot better at using human sound, visuals, and spatial navigation abilities in understanding software systems too, but I've never gotten around to implementing anything despite plenty of ideas.My latest experiment is using tones or speech synthesis articfacts to get insight into LLM operation -- ongoing resoning, tool calls, etc. Still haven't really dialed it in (hah!) to be useful yet.reply

title: Formal Verification Is Not Verifiable (alperenkeles.com)
comments:
> This allows us to (1) elide modelling the semantics of the high level programming language, we can instead model the semantics of the machine--presumably simpler semanticsISAs are pretty complicated and reasoning about programs in that context is hard which is why we have high level languages.> This distinction in terminology used to be a colloquially accepted notion, when we heard "CompCert is a formally verified compiler" or "seL4 is a formally verified microkernel" we assumed the authors did not verify vacuous or trivial properties, because the work of verification itself was held to a high standard that highly affected the reputation of the researcher.CompCert has also had extensive empirical evaluation to vet the theorems. Famously the CSmith paper (https://users.cs.utah.edu/~regehr/papers/pldi11-preprint.pdf) has this rather choice quote:>  As of early 2011, the under-development version of CompCert is the only compiler we have tested for which Csmith cannot find wrong-code errors. This is
not for lack of trying: we have devoted about six CPU-years to the task. The apparent unbreakability of CompCert supports a strong
argument that developing compiler optimizations within a proof framework, where safety checks are explicit and machine-checked,
has tangible benefits for compiler users.At my work we've extended this to CPU millennia. I hasten to add this of course doesn't rule out the possibility of poorly formed assumptions in the semantics etc (it's empirical after all) but it helps to build evidence that we have the theorems and semantic design right. More generally differential testing of this sort offers a possible way forward to build evidence in favor of theorem statements beyond expert examination.> Every discussion of formal verification must come with a list of caveats, a precise understanding of what is trusted, what is proven and what is not.Anyone that seriously participates in this work practices this. The whole community. More importantly this is precisely the point of writing down a theorem so that we can closely examine the assumptions. To abuse the CompCert example yet further it's now entirely possible to draw the envelope of assumptions, which are many for a non-toy compiler: https://arxiv.org/html/2201.10280v2.Last note, I like the kiki bouba diagram if only because it evinces the problematic "round cow" assumption and how that doesn't pan out for real software.reply

> For any first-order universally quantified property of a program we can write as a property-based test, I think we will be able to generate proofs at the binary level, against architecture models that have themselves been validated by millions of hours of testing. The challenge of extending this to multi-threaded programs, distributed systems, [..] will be years more of work we must conduct across thousands of verification engineers and researchers.I expect the distributed and concurrent version of this will come more quickly. In fact, I would be willing to bet that by EOY 2030 the bar mentioned here of single threaded software will be met for multi-threaded and distributed systems under non-adversarial failure modes. This is significantly more aggressive than most in the field (and I'm field-adjacent at best), but given the rate of progress I think it's actually a rather conservative bet (the really aggressive bet would be "July 2027").> The more "bouba" a piece of software or a given layer is, the harder it is to talk about what makes it correct. We can always talk about some correct attributes, but to talk about a uniform notion of correctness is not possible in my opinion.I largely agree with this, although I do think we're going to see more progress than expected in quantifying (and therefore verifying) usability and "look and feel" aspects of software. The risk is that this happens in a "narrow" way that forces all 'correct' software to look and feel the same, because that sameness correlates with the learned definition of 'correct'.> In solving these challenges, I think random testing and random exploration in general will prove to be invaluable tools. A test execution is a measurement, so it produces information about the real underlying system that we can leverage to falsify, harden and validate the models we use for verification. The verifiability of testing will continue to be a huge driving force of its adoption as well as a gateway into the rest of formal methods, and maybe it will even help us trust when we hear software is "formally verified" instead of wondering what was left out or when someone will find a bug in there.Strongly agree with this.reply

Love the idea of quantifying/verifying usability - maybe it isn't one thing but it's like an envelope, a 2d (or many-d) region, since we recoil at there being just one correct solution to what feels subjective and range-yreply

I don't understand how this isn't simply kicking the can. One reason I soured quickly on formal verification of programs is that it adds an immense layer of logic on top of the program (like pre/post conditions everywhere) and there's endless room in this for introducing errors.Not only is it extremely painful to write with complexity that tends to explode as programs become more complex (let alone refactored, etc), but there's no guarantee it's right, even if it's formally proven to be correct. It's just another layer of logic.Put another way, just go directly to assembly/bytecode and all you're describing is another programming language.reply
This is exactly what I've been focused on. I think Lean is one of the few, maybe only programming language expressive and powerful enough to do it effectivelyreply
That's kinda what modern programming languages are approaching. Rust for example is much closer to a specification then something like COBOL.reply

Absolute best-case scenario you've just reinvented the compiler, because in practice any sufficiently-detailed specification is going to look an awful lot like programming. Any kind of high-level plaintext "the program should not crash or get in an infinite loop" or "make the design pop" isn't going to work, after all.Even if it does work, a specification will never catch every detail. Any undergrad can come up with a formal specification for a sorting algorithm and prove that some simple ones follow it. But while both a worst-case O(n log n) Timsort and a best-case O(n^2) Selection Sort might technically be guaranteed to sort your data, the two are definitely not interchangeable!reply

When there's a language specification and everyone agrees to use it, it means that "should this code compile" has a clear meaning and so does "compiler bug."Perhaps having common packages containing shared specifications for other desirable properties will be the way to go? From the user's point of view, the tool should act like a linter.Where will trust come from? For a popular software project, it's from having a trusted team to maintain it and lots of people (and bots) watching them. first_paragraph: I may ruffle some feathers with that title; but after years as a colorist, log-encoded clips can be an unnecessary challenge. Using camera log profiles is often a crutch for location and studio set-ups. Or it’s simply used because the internet tells you log = film. That’s just not true. Many times a videographer will shoot log incorrectly – generally underexposed – expecting to ‘fix it in post’. The same issues apply to shooting in camera raw or HDR.In the video world, camera raw was introduced by the RED Digital Cinema Camera Company in 2007, borrowing from still photo concepts. Log (logarithmic) videography came to the forefront when ARRI introduced the Alexa in 2010, which offered a Log-C profile. ARRI’s camera raw format wasn’t post-friendly, so Log-C was a better fit.
